title: Capacity Planning
subtitle: Back-of-the-envelope resource modeling, peak-to-average provisioning, IOPS vs bandwidth sizing, and load testing.
keyTakeaways: Never provision for average QPS: calculate Daily Average -> Peak Diurnal Factor (2x-4x) -> Flash Event Multiplier (2x-5x) -> N-1 AZ Failover Headroom (+50%).
Separate Storage Capacity (TB), Storage IOPS (random 4KB reads/writes), and Network/Disk Throughput (MB/s sequential scans)—any one of the three can be the binding limit.

Validate mathematical capacity models empirically via Production Shadowing or Controlled Load Tests (Squeeze Testing) that intentionally push single pods to their breaking point to establish true unit capacity.

sections.heading: 1. Architectural Fundamentals & Core Mechanics
sections.body: Capacity Planning is a foundational architectural concept in distributed systems. Back-of-the-envelope resource modeling, peak-to-average provisioning, IOPS vs bandwidth sizing, and load testing. Fundamentally, Capacity planning translates product metrics (DAU, retention, media size) into concrete hardware primitives (vCPUs, RAM working-set size, SSD IOPS, and NIC bandwidth). Using powers-of-two approximations and standard constants keeps mental math fast and accurate.
bullets: **Core Architectural Principle**: Never provision for average QPS: calculate Daily Average -> Peak Diurnal Factor (2x-4x) -> Flash Event Multiplier (2x-5x) -> N-1 AZ Failover Headroom (+50%).

**Problem Space & Invariants**: Separate Storage Capacity (TB), Storage IOPS (random 4KB reads/writes), and Network/Disk Throughput (MB/s sequential scans)—any one of the three can be the binding limit.
**System Boundary**: Operates across client network dispatch, gateway queuing, thread execution pools, and persistent storage I/O.

sections.heading: 2. Architectural Patterns & Implementation Topologies
sections.body: In production distributed systems, capacity planning manifests across several distinct architectural classifications, operational modes, and implementation strategies:
bullets: **Static N+1 Peak Provisioning**: Focuses on guaranteed instant capacity for flash spikes and az failures; zero auto-scaling cold-start risk. Best suited for Stateful storage clusters (Cassandra, Kafka, Redis), core auth, and latency-critical Tier-0 gateways..

**Dynamic Elastic Sizing with Spot/Preemptible Pools**: Focuses on reduces compute spend by 50-70% by matching instance count tightly to hourly demand curves. Best suited for Stateless worker tiers, async media transcoding, CI/CD runners, and ML batch pipelines..

Time & Traffic Constants: $1\text{ day} = 86,400\text{s} \approx 10^5\text{s}$. Therefore, $100\text{M requests/day} \approx 1,000\text{ RPS average}$. $1\text{ year} \approx 3.15 \times 10^7\text{s}$.

Working-Set RAM Sizing (The 20% Rule): You do not need to fit 100 TB of historical rows into Redis/DB Buffer Pool—only the hot active working set (typically the last 24-72 hours or top 15-20% of entities by Pareto distribution).

Replication & Index Amplification: A single logical user write of 1 KB to a database with 4 secondary B-Tree indexes and 3x replication factor generates $1 \times (1 + 4) \times 3 = 15$ physical disk I/O operations!

IOPS vs Bandwidth Ceiling: A cloud EBS gp3 volume might have plenty of free terabytes, but if it is provisioned for 3,000 IOPS, a burst of 8,000 random 4KB point-reads/sec will throttle disk latency from 1ms to 50ms+.

sections.heading: 3. Production Strengths: Where & How to Apply
sections.body: Adopting appropriate design patterns around capacity planning unlocks critical performance, scalability, and operational advantages for modern backend platforms:
bullets: **Where to Use — High-Impact Scenarios**: Optimal for Stateful storage clusters (Cassandra, Kafka, Redis), core auth, and latency-critical Tier-0 gateways. and environments requiring Guaranteed instant capacity for flash spikes and AZ failures; zero auto-scaling cold-start risk..

**Where to Use — High-Throughput Scenarios**: Recommended for Stateless worker tiers, async media transcoding, CI/CD runners, and ML batch pipelines. where Reduces compute spend by 50-70% by matching instance count tightly to hourly demand curves..

**How to Use — Engineering Implementation**: A common capacity planning mistake is calculating raw disk space (`1 TB/day * 365 = 365 TB/year`) while ignoring **IOPS limits** and **Write Amplification**.. Always establish explicit thresholds, measurement baselines, and automated monitoring.
**Architectural Leverage**: Provides predictable resource boundaries, bounds blast radius, and optimizes cost per transaction.

sections.heading: 4. Failure Modes & Trade-Offs: When to Avoid
sections.body: While essential for scalable engineering, capacity planning introduces substantial architectural trade-offs, operational failure modes, and anti-patterns if applied inappropriately:
bullets: **Where to Avoid — Trade-Off Bottlenecks**: Avoid when constraints impose cluster runs at 20-35% average utilization during off-peak hours, increasing baseline compute cost.
**Where to Avoid — Complexity Ceiling**: Avoid premature optimization when vulnerable to simultaneous spot instance reclamation and auto-scaling lag during vertical spikes.
**Catastrophic Failure Modes**: Uncalibrated parameters can trigger queue exhaustion, thread starvation, cascading retry storms, and tail latency amplification.
**Operational Overhead**: Requires continuous observability (p95/p99 latency tracking, saturation alerts, and distributed tracing across hop boundaries).

sections.heading: 5. Staff+ Engineering Verdict & Interview Playbook
sections.body: Mastering capacity planning is a defining trait of Staff-level distributed systems engineers. Navigating the delicate balance between performance, reliability, and simplicity ensures architectures scale sustainably without introducing unmanageable operational friction.
bullets: **Staff+ Golden Rule**: Validate mathematical capacity models empirically via Production Shadowing or Controlled Load Tests (Squeeze Testing) that intentionally push single pods to their breaking point to establish true unit capacity.

**Staff+ Interview Playbook**: Structure your interview capacity math into 4 crisp lines: (1) Traffic (Avg & Peak RPS), (2) Bandwidth (Ingress/Egress MB/s), (3) Memory (Hot working set in Redis), and (4) Storage (Daily growth x Replication factor x Retention years)—then actively use those numbers to pick your sharding strategy!
